answer.rationale: The recovered source records expose a systematic problem with the inherited memory layer: memory_73 ('targeted promotional pricing is effective ... strong acquisition and revenue lift') is a lossy summary of exp_73, which actually showed 30-day retention -12% and an explicit instruction NOT to generalize discounting as sustainable growth. Since one consolidated memory demonstrably dropped the disconfirming half of its source, the other unverified consolidations (memory_31, memory_44, memory_57, memory_91) must be treated as possibly similarly optimistic until their archived sources are re-pulled next week. That leaves memory_86 as the only claim corroborated by a recovered primary record (exp_86: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%, conclusion confirmed), and it is the only direction with positive evidence on retention rather than acquisition. Against a competitor price cut, matching with promotional_pricing is precisely the move exp_73 warns against: it would buy signups from the same price-sensitive SMB cohort that does not survive first renewal, inflating near-term qualified revenue while degrading the sustainable long-term revenue that is the stated primary objective. I therefore act on shortened onboarding to deepen time-to-value for the at-risk SMB base. I scope it as a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout because exp_86 was run in a normal-demand context, not a competitor-price-shock context, and I have no verification budget left to check that transfer; the test should be instrumented for retention and renewal, not just completion, so it does not repeat exp_73's error of reading an acquisition metric as a durability signal. Referral incentive (memory_57) is the most plausible second option and may well be right, but its source is unverified and it presumes healthy retention among the referring base, which is exactly what is currently in question.
